⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: Cell address galat samajhna → B3 matlab Column B, Row 3 — not row B, column 3.
    Fix: Hamesha yaad rakho: Column letter PEHLE, Row number BAAD mein.
  • Mistake: Sheets rename na karna → Sheet1, Sheet2 se kaam chalana — later confusion hota hai.
    Fix: Sheet tab pe double-click karke meaningful naam do: "Employee Data", "Reports".
  • Mistake: Data ke beech mein blank rows rakhna → Sorting, Filtering, Pivot sab break ho jayega.
    Fix: Data continuous hona chahiye — koi blank row beech mein nahi.

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: What is the maximum number of rows and columns in Excel?
Ans: Excel supports maximum 10,48,576 rows (2^20) and 16,384 columns (2^14, A to XFD). This means a single Excel sheet can hold approximately 17 billion cells. However, practical performance limits are much lower depending on system RAM and data complexity.

Q2: What is the difference between a Workbook and a Worksheet?
Ans: A Workbook is the entire Excel file (.xlsx) — like a notebook. A Worksheet (Sheet) is a single page inside the workbook — like a page in the notebook. One workbook can contain multiple worksheets. Each worksheet has its own grid of cells, data, and formulas. Default workbook opens with one sheet (Sheet1).

Q3: What is a Cell Range? Give examples.
Ans: A Cell Range is a group of selected cells referenced as start:end. Examples: A1:A10 (column range — 10 cells in column A), A1:E1 (row range — 5 cells in row 1), A1:C5 (block range — 3 columns × 5 rows = 15 cells), A:A (entire column A), 1:1 (entire row 1). Ranges are used in formulas like SUM(A1:A10).

2. Data Entry — Text, Numbers, Dates

text

🔍 Definition: Data Entry in Excel involves typing values into cells. Excel automatically detects the data type: Text (left-aligned by default), Numbers (right-aligned), Dates (right-aligned, stored as serial numbers internally), and Formulas (start with = sign). Understanding data types is critical because wrong types cause formula errors.

🎯 Samjho Simple Bhasha Mein: Excel smart hai — tum jo type karte ho woh automatically samajh leta hai. "Rahul" likho toh text samjhega (left align). "75000" likho toh number samjhega (right align). "15-Mar-2021" likho toh date samjhega. Lekin kabhi kabhi galti hoti hai — "001" likho toh "1" ban jaata hai (leading zeros hat jaate hain). Isliye data types samajhna zaroori hai.

💡 Data Types in Excel:

Text: Names, IDs, Codes — Left aligned by default
Number: Salary, Age, Quantity — Right aligned, math possible
Date: Dates — Stored as serial numbers (1-Jan-1900 = 1)
Formula: Starts with = sign — calculates result
Boolean: TRUE or FALSE
Error: #VALUE!, #REF!, #N/A, #DIV/0!

⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: Phone number type karna → "09876543210" ka "0" hat jaata hai, sirf "9876543210" bachta hai.
    Fix: Pehle cell ko Text format karo (Right-click → Format Cells → Text) ya ' (apostrophe) se shuru karo: '09876543210
  • Mistake: Date ko text format mein type karna → "15-Mar-2021" text ban gaya toh formulas kaam nahi karenge.
    Fix: Cell right-aligned ho toh date hai, left-aligned ho toh text hai. Text hai toh DATEVALUE() se convert karo.
  • Mistake: Numbers ke aage space dena → " 75000" — yeh text ban jaata hai!
    Fix: Number cells mein extra spaces mat daalo. TRIM() function se clean karo.
  • Mistake: Formula type karte waqt = bhool jaana → "SUM(A1:A10)" text ban jayega.
    Fix: Har formula = se shuru hona chahiye: =SUM(A1:A10)

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: How does Excel store dates internally?
Ans: Excel stores dates as serial numbers starting from January 1, 1900 (serial number 1). Each subsequent day adds 1 to the serial number. For example: 1-Jan-1900 = 1, 1-Feb-1900 = 32, 15-Mar-2021 = 44270. This numeric storage allows date arithmetic — subtracting two dates gives the number of days between them.

Q2: How to preserve leading zeros in Excel (like employee codes 001, 002)?
Ans: Three methods: (1) Format cell as Text before entering data (Right-click → Format Cells → Text). (2) Prefix with apostrophe: type '001 — apostrophe won't display but forces text treatment. (3) Use Custom Number Format: 000 — this displays 1 as 001, 2 as 002 automatically while keeping the underlying value as a number.

Q3: What is the difference between Enter and Tab when typing data?
Ans: Enter confirms the entry and moves the cursor DOWN to the next row — used when filling a column. Tab confirms the entry and moves the cursor RIGHT to the next column — used when filling a row. Shift+Enter moves UP, Shift+Tab moves LEFT. Ctrl+Enter confirms but stays in the same cell.

text

It includes font styling (bold, italic, size, color), cell appearance (background color, borders, alignment), and cell structure (merge, wrap text, row height, column width). Good formatting makes data readable and professional.

🎯 Samjho Simple Bhasha Mein: Formatting matlab data ko sundar banana. Jaise ek plain white wall hai — paint karo, frames lagao, toh achhi dikhti hai. Excel mein bhi — headers bold karo, background color do, borders lagao — professional report ban jaati hai. Lekin yaad rakhna — formatting sirf dikhawa hai, actual data nahi badalta. 75000 ko bold karo toh woh dikhne mein alag lagega but value same rahegi.

⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: Merge & Center overuse karna → Merged cells sorting, filtering, formulas sab break kar dete hain.
    Fix: Sirf title row mein Merge use karo. Data area mein kabhi Merge mat karo!
  • Mistake: Manual column width set karna har baar → Time waste.
    Fix: Ctrl+A → Format → AutoFit Column Width — ek baar mein sab adjust.
  • Mistake: Colors ka overdose — rainbow spreadsheet banana → Professional nahi dikhta, eye strain hota hai.
    Fix: Maximum 2-3 colors use karo. Headers dark, data light. Alternating row colors subtle rakhna.

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: What is the difference between Merge & Center and Center Across Selection?
Ans: Merge & Center physically combines multiple cells into one large cell — this breaks sorting, filtering and formulas that reference those cells. Center Across Selection (Format Cells → Alignment → Horizontal: Center Across Selection) visually centers text across cells WITHOUT merging them — individual cells remain intact. Center Across Selection is the professional alternative to Merge for headers.

Q2: Does formatting change the actual cell value?
Ans: No, formatting only changes how data is displayed — not the underlying value. A cell showing ₹75,000 still contains the number 75000 internally. A cell formatted as percentage showing 50% actually contains 0.5. This distinction is important because formulas always work with the actual value, not the displayed format.

4. Number Formatting — Currency, Percentage, Date Format

text

🔍 Definition: Number Formatting controls how numeric values are displayed. You can show numbers as Currency (₹75,000), Percentage (50%), Dates (15-Mar-2021), Accounting format, Scientific notation, or Custom formats — all without changing the underlying value.

🎯 Samjho Simple Bhasha Mein: Number formatting matlab "number dikhega kaise." 75000 ko "₹75,000" ya "75,000.00" ya "75K" — sab formatting se hota hai. Actual value 75000 hi rehti hai. Date 44270 hai but dikhta hai "15-Mar-2021" — yeh bhi formatting hai. Custom format se apne mann ka display bana sakte ho — "75000" ko "75 Thousand" bhi dikha sakte ho!

⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: Percentage format mein 15 type karna → 1500% dikhega! (Excel 15 ko 15*100=1500% banata hai).
    Fix: Percentage ke liye 0.15 type karo → 15% dikhega. Ya pehle type karo, phir format lagao.
  • Mistake: ₹ symbol manually type karna → Formulas break ho sakte hain.
    Fix: Currency format use karo (Ctrl+1 → Currency → ₹ symbol select karo). Manually ₹ mat likho.
  • Mistake: Date format regional settings ke hisaab se change hona → US mein mm/dd/yyyy, India mein dd/mm/yyyy.
    Fix: Custom format explicitly set karo: dd-mmm-yyyy — yeh worldwide unambiguous hai.

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: What is the difference between Currency and Accounting number format?
Ans: Currency format places the currency symbol directly next to the number: ₹75,000. Accounting format aligns currency symbols at the left edge of the cell and the numbers at the right: ₹ 75,000. Accounting also shows negative values in parentheses (75,000) instead of -₹75,000. Accounting format is preferred in financial reports for clean column alignment.

Q2: How to create a custom format that shows negative numbers in red?
Ans: Custom format code has up to 4 sections separated by semicolons: positive;negative;zero;text. For red negatives: #,##0;[Red]-#,##0;0;"Text". The [Red] color code makes negative values appear in red. Other colors: [Blue], [Green], [Yellow], [Magenta], [Cyan]. Example: #,##0;[Red](#,##0) shows negatives in red with parentheses.

Q3: What is the difference between # and 0 in custom number format?
Ans: # displays a digit only if it exists — no leading or trailing zeros: ###.## shows 5 as "5." (no extra zeros). 0 always displays a digit — fills with zero if needed: 000.00 shows 5 as "005.00". Use # when extra zeros are not needed (general numbers). Use 0 when exact decimal places or leading zeros are required (employee codes, financial figures).

5. Cell References — Relative, Absolute & Mixed

text

🔍 Definition: Cell References determine how a formula behaves when copied to other cells. Relative Reference (A1) changes when copied — both row and column adjust. Absolute Reference ($A$1) stays fixed when copied — never changes. Mixed Reference ($A1 or A$1) locks either column or row while the other adjusts.

🎯 Samjho Simple Bhasha Mein: Socho tumne cell H2 mein formula likha: =E2*12 (annual salary). Ab is formula ko H3, H4... mein copy karo. Relative reference automatically adjust hoga — H3 mein =E3*12, H4 mein =E4*12. But agar tax rate cell K1 mein hai aur formula =E2*K1 hai — copy karne par K1 bhi shift ho jayega K2, K3... jo wrong hai! Fix: =E2*$K$1 — dollar sign lock kar deta hai.

💡 Cell Reference Types:

Relative (A1): Dono change hote hain → Copy down: A1→A2→A3
Absolute ($A$1): Kuch change nahi → Copy anywhere: $A$1 hi rahega
Mixed ($A1): Column locked, Row changes → $A1→$A2→$A3
Mixed (A$1): Row locked, Column changes → A$1→B$1→C$1

Shortcut: F4 key se toggle karo: A1 → $A$1 → A$1 → $A1 → A1

💻 Real-World Examples:

=E212 → H2: =E212 → 7500012 = 900000
→ H3: =E312 → 8500012 = 1020000 (auto adjust!)
→ H4: =E412 → 48000*12 = 576000

// ============ ABSOLUTE REFERENCE ============
// Tax rate in cell K1 = 30% (0.30)
// Cell I2: Tax Amount
=E2*$K$1 → I2: =E2*$K$1 → 750000.30 = 22500
→ I3: =E3$K$1 → 850000.30 = 25500 (K1 fixed!)
→ I4: =E4$K$1 → 48000*0.30 = 14400

// WITHOUT $ (WRONG!):
=E2K1 → I2: =E2K1 → 750000.30 = 22500 ✅
→ I3: =E3K2 → 85000*??? → K2 empty! ERROR! ❌

// ============ MIXED REFERENCE ============
// Multiplication Table example
// Row 1: 1,2,3,4,5 (B1:F1)
// Column A: 1,2,3,4,5 (A2:A6)
// Cell B2 formula:
=$A2B$1 → B2: =$A2B$1 → 11 = 1
→ C2: =$A2C$1 → 12 = 2 (column changes, $A stays)
→ B3: =$A3B$1 → 21 = 2 (row changes, $1 stays)
→ C3: =$A3C$1 → 2*2 = 4

→ Press F4 → A$1 (Mixed — row locked)

Reference Type Syntax Copy Down Copy Right Use Case
Relative A1 A2, A3, A4 B1, C1, D1 Same formula per row
Absolute $A$1 $A$1, $A$1 $A$1, $A$1 Tax rate, constants

⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: Tax rate, discount rate jaise constants mein $ na lagana → Copy karne par reference shift ho jaata hai → Wrong calculations!
    Fix: Constants ke liye hamesha $A$1 (absolute) use karo.
  • Mistake: $ manually type karna → Slow aur error-prone.
    Fix: Cell reference pe cursor rakho aur F4 dabao — automatic toggle hoga.
  • Mistake: Mixed reference kab use karna hai samajh na aana.
    Fix: Rule: "Kya lock karna hai wahan $ lagao." Column fix chahiye → $A. Row fix chahiye → $1.

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: What is the difference between Relative and Absolute cell reference?
Ans: Relative reference (A1) changes when formula is copied — row and column adjust relative to the new position. Absolute reference ($A$1) never changes when copied — it always points to the same cell. Use relative when each row needs its own calculation (like salary*12 for each employee). Use absolute when referencing a fixed value (like tax rate in cell K1).

Q2: What is a Mixed Reference and when do you use it?
Ans: Mixed reference locks either the column ($A1) or the row (A$1) while the other adjusts. $A1 means column A is always fixed but row changes when copied down. A$1 means row 1 is always fixed but column changes when copied right. Classic use case: multiplication table where you need one axis to stay fixed and the other to move.

Q3: How do you toggle between reference types quickly?
Ans: Place cursor on the cell reference inside a formula and press F4 repeatedly. It cycles through: A1 (relative) → $A$1 (absolute) → A$1 (mixed row) → $A1 (mixed column) → back to A1. This is much faster than manually typing dollar signs and reduces errors.

Q4: Give a real-world example where you would need $A1 vs A$1.
Ans: $A1 (column locked): Creating a report where column A has employee names — copy formula right to add salary, department etc. but always reference column A for names. A$1 (row locked): Headers in row 1 — copy formula down for each employee but always reference row 1 for column headers (like month names in a budget template).

6. Basic Formulas — SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT

🔍 Definition: Excel formulas always start with the equals sign (=). Basic formulas include SUM (total), AVERAGE (mean), MIN (smallest), MAX (largest), and COUNT (number of numeric cells). These aggregate functions work on a range of cells and return a single value.

🎯 Samjho Simple Bhasha Mein: Formulas Excel ki jaan hain. SUM matlab "sab jod do", AVERAGE matlab "average nikalo", MIN matlab "sabse chhota dhundho", MAX matlab "sabse bada dhundho", COUNT matlab "kitne numbers hain gino." Yeh sab ek range par kaam karte hain — jaise =SUM(E2:E11) matlab E2 se E11 tak sabki salary jod do.

💡 Formula Syntax:

=SUM(range) → Total jod
=AVERAGE(range) → Average
=MIN(range) → Sabse chhoti value
=MAX(range) → Sabse badi value
=COUNT(range) → Kitne numeric cells
=COUNTA(range) → Kitne non-empty cells
=COUNTBLANK(range) → Kitne blank cells

Shortcut: Alt + = → AutoSum

💻 Real-World Examples:

// SUM — Total Salary Cell E12: =SUM(E2:E11) → 683000
// AVERAGE — Average Salary
Cell E13: =AVERAGE(E2:E11) → 68300

// MIN & MAX
Cell E14: =MIN(E2:E11) → 45000 (Kavita)
Cell E15: =MAX(E2:E11) → 95000 (Anjali)

// COUNT & COUNTA
=COUNT(A2:A11) → 10 (numbers only)
=COUNTA(B2:B11) → 10 (non-empty)

// Salary Range
=MAX(E2:E11)-MIN(E2:E11) → 50000

⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: Header row include karna → =SUM(E1:E11)
    Fix: =SUM(E2:E11) — data row se shuru karo.
  • Mistake: COUNT aur COUNTA confuse karna.
    Fix: Names count → COUNTA, salary count → COUNT.
  • Mistake: AVERAGE mein 0 aur blank ka behavior na samajhna.
    Fix: AVERAGE blank ignore karta hai but 0 count karta hai.

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: Difference between COUNT, COUNTA, COUNTBLANK?
Ans: COUNT = numeric cells only. COUNTA = all non-empty. COUNTBLANK = empty cells only. [10, "Hi", "", 20, ""] → COUNT=2, COUNTA=3, COUNTBLANK=2.

Q2: AVERAGE blank vs zero?
Ans: AVERAGE ignores blanks but includes 0. [10,20,blank,30] → AVG=20. [10,20,0,30] → AVG=15.

Q3: AutoSum shortcut?
Ans: Alt + = automatically inserts SUM for adjacent range.

7. AutoFill & Flash Fill

🔍 Definition: AutoFill fills cells with a pattern by dragging the fill handle (small square at bottom-right of cell). Flash Fill (Ctrl+E) is Excel's AI — detects patterns from examples and fills automatically. Available in Excel 2013+.

🎯 Samjho Simple Bhasha Mein: AutoFill matlab "pattern samajh ke aage fill karo." 1, 2 likho drag karo — 3, 4, 5 automatic! January drag karo — February, March automatic! Flash Fill aur smart hai — ek example do, Ctrl+E dabao, baaki Excel khud samajh jaata hai.

💡 AutoFill Patterns:

Numbers: 1, 2 → drag → 3, 4, 5...
Even: 2, 4 → drag → 6, 8, 10...
Dates: Jan → drag → Feb, Mar...
Days: Mon → drag → Tue, Wed...
Text+Num: Emp001 → drag → Emp002, Emp003...
Formulas: =E2*12 → drag → =E3*12...
Flash Fill: Ctrl + E

💻 AutoFill Examples:

// Number Series: A1: 1 A2: 2 → Drag → 3, 4, 5... A1: 2 A2: 4 → Drag → 6, 8, 10... A1: 100 A2: 200 → Drag → 300, 400...
// Dates & Days:
A1: January → Drag → February, March...
A1: Monday → Drag → Tuesday, Wednesday...
A1: Q1 → Drag → Q2, Q3, Q4...

// Text + Number:
A1: Emp001 → Drag → Emp002, Emp003...
A1: Week 1 → Drag → Week 2, Week 3...

💻 Flash Fill Examples (Ctrl+E):

// Extract First Name: B: "Rahul Sharma" H: "Rahul" ← Manual B: "Priya Singh" H: [empty] ← Ctrl+E → AUTO!
// Create Email:
A: Rahul B: Sharma H: rahul.sharma@co.com ← Manual
A: Priya B: Singh H: [empty] ← Ctrl+E → AUTO!

// Format Phone:
A: 9876543210 H: +91-98765-43210 ← Manual
A: 8765432109 H: [empty] ← Ctrl+E → AUTO!

📊 AutoFill Options (after dragging):

  • Copy Cells: Same value repeat
  • Fill Series: Pattern continue (default)
  • Fill Formatting Only: Only format, no data
  • Fill Weekdays: Skip weekends!
  • Fill Months: Month-wise jump

⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: Sirf ek cell se drag bina Ctrl → Same value repeat.
    Fix: 2 cells mein pattern likho phir drag. Ya Ctrl hold karke drag.
  • Mistake: Flash Fill kaam na kare.
    Fix: Ek clear example do, phir Ctrl+E. Data → Flash Fill bhi try karo.
  • Mistake: AutoFill se formula copy without checking references.
    Fix: Absolute reference chahiye toh $ lagao (F4).

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: AutoFill vs Flash Fill?
Ans: AutoFill continues patterns by dragging — numbers, dates, formulas. Flash Fill (Ctrl+E) is AI-powered — recognizes complex patterns from examples. Flash Fill can extract, combine, reformat text.

Q2: Fill weekdays only?
Ans: Type date, drag fill handle, click AutoFill Options icon → "Fill Weekdays." Skips Saturday and Sunday.

8. Sorting & Filtering

🔍 Definition: Sorting rearranges data rows in ascending or descending order. Filtering hides rows that don't match criteria. Sorting changes order; Filtering changes visibility.

🎯 Samjho Simple Bhasha Mein: Sorting matlab "data arrange karo" — salary highest first ya naam A to Z. Filtering matlab "sirf woh dikhao jo chahiye" — sirf IT department. Sorting se saari rows dikhti hain, filtering se kuch chhup jaati hain.

💡 Shortcuts:

Ctrl + Shift + L → Toggle Filter on/off
Alt + D + S → Sort dialog box
Alt + ↓ → Open filter dropdown

💻 Sorting Examples:

// Single Column Sort: → Click Salary column → Data → Sort Largest to Smallest → Result: Anjali(95K), Sneha(92K), Priya(85K)...
// Multi-Level Sort:
→ Data → Sort dialog
→ Level 1: Dept (A to Z)
→ Add Level → Level 2: Salary (Largest to Smallest)
→ Result: Within each dept, salary high to low

💻 Filtering Examples:

// Enable Filter: Ctrl + Shift + L
// Text Filter — IT department only:
→ Dept dropdown → Uncheck All → Check "IT" → OK

// Number Filter — Salary > 70000:
→ Salary dropdown → Number Filters → Greater Than → 70000

// Multiple Filters:
→ Filter Dept = "IT" + Filter Salary > 80000
→ Result: Sneha(92K), Anjali(95K)

// Clear: Data → Clear or Ctrl+Shift+L toggle

⚡ Important: SUM/COUNT filtered data par hidden rows bhi include karte hain! Sirf visible cells ka sum chahiye toh =SUBTOTAL(9, E2:E11) use karo.

⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: Data mein blank row → Sort/filter incomplete.
    Fix: Beech mein blank row mat rakhna.
  • Mistake: Sirf ek column select karke sort → Columns mismatch!
    Fix: Kisi bhi cell mein click karke sort — Excel auto-detect karega.
  • Mistake: Filtered data par SUM → Hidden rows bhi count.
    Fix: =SUBTOTAL(9, E2:E11) use karo.

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: Sorting vs Filtering?
Ans: Sorting rearranges ALL rows — order changes. Filtering hides non-matching — data stays, visibility changes. Sorting permanent, filtering temporary.

Q2: Multi-column sort?
Ans: Data → Sort → Add Level. Level 1 sorts first, Level 2 within each group. Up to 64 levels.

Q3: Sum visible cells only?
Ans: =SUBTOTAL(9, range). 9=SUM, 1=AVG, 2=COUNT, 4=MAX, 5=MIN. Ignores hidden rows.

9. Find & Replace

🔍 Definition: Find (Ctrl+F) searches for text, numbers, or formatting. Replace (Ctrl+H) finds values and substitutes them. Both support wildcards (* and ?) for pattern matching.

🎯 Samjho Simple Bhasha Mein: Find & Replace ek smart search tool hai. 1000 rows mein "Delhi" ko "New Delhi" banana hai — Ctrl+H se ek click mein sab change! Wildcards se "R*" likhoge toh Rahul, Ravi, Rohit sab milenge.

💡 Shortcuts & Wildcards:

Ctrl + F → Find
Ctrl + H → Replace
* → Any number of characters
? → Exactly one character
~* → Search literal asterisk
~? → Search literal question mark

💻 Real-World Examples:

// Basic Replace: Ctrl+H → Find: "Delhi" → Replace: "New Delhi" → Replace All → "3 replacements made"
// Wildcard Search:
Find: R* → Rahul, Ravi, Rohit
Find: *Kumar → Amit Kumar, Rahul Kumar
Find: R?vi → Ravi (not Rahul)

// Advanced Options (Ctrl+F → Options):
Within: Sheet / Workbook
Look in: Formulas / Values / Comments
☑ Match case → "delhi" ≠ "Delhi"
☑ Match entire cell → "IT" exact (not "ITEM")

// Remove line breaks:
Find: Ctrl+J Replace: [empty] → Replace All

⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: "Match entire cell" check na karna → "IT" search mein "ITEM", "CITY" bhi match.
    Fix: Exact match chahiye toh check karo.
  • Mistake: Replace All bina verify kiye → Galat replacement.
    Fix: Pehle "Find All" karke verify karo.
  • Mistake: Formula search mein "Look in: Values" selected → Formula text nahi milega.
    Fix: "Look in: Formulas" select karo.

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: Wildcards in Excel Find?
Ans: * matches any number of characters. ? matches exactly one. ~* searches literal asterisk. "R*" finds Rahul, Ravi, R.

Q2: Search across all sheets?
Ans: Ctrl+F → Options → Within: "Workbook" instead of "Sheet". Find All shows matches from all sheets.

Q3: Replace formatting?
Ans: Ctrl+H → Options → Format button next to Find/Replace. Select Bold → Regular. Replace All removes all bold formatting.

10. Freeze Panes & Split View

🔍 Definition: Freeze Panes locks specific rows/columns so they remain visible while scrolling. Split View divides the worksheet into separate panes that scroll independently. Both help navigate large datasets.

🎯 Samjho Simple Bhasha Mein: 1000 employees ki table mein neeche scroll karo toh header chhup jaata hai. Freeze Panes se header lock kar do — kitna bhi scroll karo, headers hamesha dikhenge. Split View se ek sheet mein do jagah ka data ek saath dekh sakte ho!

💡 Freeze Panes Options:

Freeze Top Row: Row 1 (header) lock — sabse common!
Freeze First Column: Column A lock
Freeze Panes (Custom): Selected cell ke UPAR aur LEFT freeze
Unfreeze: View → Unfreeze Panes

Rule: Jo cell select karo — uske UPAR rows aur LEFT columns freeze!

💻 Step-by-Step Guide:

// FREEZE TOP ROW (Most Common): → View → Freeze Panes → "Freeze Top Row" → Row 1 headers always visible while scrolling!
// FREEZE FIRST COLUMN:
→ View → Freeze Panes → "Freeze First Column"
→ Column A always visible while scrolling right!

// FREEZE BOTH (Row 1 + Column A):
→ Click cell B2 (below row 1, right of col A)
→ View → Freeze Panes → "Freeze Panes"
→ Row 1 AND Column A both frozen!

// FREEZE MULTIPLE ROWS (top 3):
→ Click cell A4 (below what you want frozen)
→ View → Freeze Panes → "Freeze Panes"
→ Rows 1, 2, 3 frozen!

// UNFREEZE:
→ View → Freeze Panes → "Unfreeze Panes"

// SPLIT VIEW:
→ Click cell → View → Split
→ Window divides into independent panes
→ View → Split again → Remove split

// NEW WINDOW (same file, 2 views):
→ View → New Window → View → Arrange All

📊 Freeze Panes — Visual Guide:

🔹 Freeze Top Row: Row 1 (Header) stays visible. Rows 2, 3, 4... scroll normally.

🔹 Freeze First Column: Column A stays visible. Columns B, C, D... scroll normally.

🔹 Freeze Both: Click B2 → Freeze Panes. Row 1 aur Column A dono lock. Baaki data scroll hota hai — headers aur IDs hamesha visible!

🔹 Split View: Screen 2 ya 4 parts mein divide. Har part independently scroll hoti hai. Row 1 aur Row 500 dono ek saath dekh sakte ho!

⚠️ Common Mistakes:

  • Mistake: Galat cell select karke Freeze → Wrong rows/columns freeze.
    Fix: Rule: selected cell ke UPAR rows, LEFT columns freeze. Row 1 ke liye A2 select karo.
  • Mistake: Freeze aur Split confuse karna.
    Fix: Headers lock → Freeze. Two areas compare → Split.
  • Mistake: Freeze print mein repeat nahi hota.
    Fix: Print mein headers: Page Layout → Print Titles → Rows to repeat: $1:$1

💬 Interview Questions:

Q1: What is Freeze Panes?
Ans: Locks rows/columns so they stay visible while scrolling. Three options: Freeze Top Row, Freeze First Column, Freeze Panes (custom based on selected cell). Unfreeze: View → Unfreeze Panes.

Q2: Freeze vs Split?
Ans: Freeze locks rows/columns in fixed position — frozen area never scrolls. Split divides window into independent panes — each scrolls separately. Use Freeze for headers, Split for comparing different areas.

Q3: Freeze both row 1 AND column A?
Ans: Click cell B2 (intersection of unfrozen area) → View → Freeze Panes. Row 1 (above B2) and Column A (left of B2) both freeze. Key is selecting correct cell — always at intersection.

Q4: Freeze Panes print mein kaam karta hai?
Ans: No, Freeze is only for screen navigation. For printing headers on every page: Page Layout → Print Titles → Rows to repeat at top: $1:$1.

Part 1 Complete — Excel Basics Quick Reference

TopicKey ShortcutPurpose
InterfaceCtrl+HomeGo to A1
Data EntryCtrl+;Insert date
FormattingCtrl+1Format Cells
Number FormatCtrl+Shift+4Currency
Cell ReferencesF4Toggle $ reference
Basic FormulasAlt+=AutoSum
AutoFillCtrl+EFlash Fill
Sort & FilterCtrl+Shift+LToggle filter
Find & ReplaceCtrl+F / Ctrl+HFind / Replace
Freeze PanesView → FreezeLock headers

🎯 Top 20 Excel Shortcuts — Yaad Kar Lo!

Ctrl+C CopyCtrl+S Save
Ctrl+V PasteCtrl+Z Undo
Ctrl+X CutCtrl+Y Redo
Ctrl+A Select AllCtrl+P Print
Ctrl+B BoldCtrl+1 Format Cells
Ctrl+F FindCtrl+H Replace
Ctrl+Shift+L FilterAlt+= AutoSum
Ctrl+; DateCtrl+E Flash Fill
F2 Edit CellF4 Toggle $
Ctrl+Home Go A1Ctrl+End Last Cell

Next: Data Insights Excel Masterclass — Part 2

Part 2 mein hum cover karenge: Lookup & Reference Functions — VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, INDEX, MATCH, INDEX+MATCH combo, XLOOKUP, CHOOSE, INDIRECT, OFFSET, ROW/COLUMN — Data Insights par.

Happy Learning & Keep Excelling! 🚀

File Handling & Exceptions
entry.content:
Data Insights Python Handbook — Part 9

File Handling & Exceptions 📁

Python mein files kaise handle karte hain aur errors se kaise deal karte hain. File modes se lekar custom exceptions tak, CSV/JSON handling se lekar try-except patterns tak — 13 topics Basic se Advanced tak. Employee data ke real examples aur interview Q&A ke saath. Data Insights par.

📑 Is Chapter Mein Kya Sikhenge:

  • 🟢 Basic: File Introduction, Open/Close, Reading Files
  • 🟡 Medium: Writing Files, with Statement, CSV & JSON
  • 🔴 Advanced: File Paths (os, pathlib), Exception Handling
  • 🔴 Advanced: Common Exceptions, Raising & Custom Exceptions
  • 📋 Summary: Best Practices & Patterns

📊 Sample Data — Employee Records

Is chapter ke examples Employee CSV/JSON files par based honge. Sample file employees.csv:

id,name,department,salary
101,Aarav,IT,55000
102,Ishita,HR,72000
103,Kabir,Finance,65000
104,Diya,IT,58000
105,Rohan,Marketing,80000

1. File Handling Introduction — Text vs Binary, File Modes 🟢

📘 Definition: File Handling is the process of reading from, writing to, and manipulating files stored on disk. Python provides built-in open() function to work with files. Files are of two types — Text files (.txt, .csv, .json — human-readable) and Binary files (.jpg, .mp3, .exe — machine-readable bytes). File Mode decides what operation you can perform.

🎯 Samjho Hinglish Mein: File handling = files ke saath kaam karna — padhna, likhna, update karna. Text files mein readable characters hote hain (jaise notepad mein khulti hain). Binary files mein raw bytes hote hain (images, videos). Python mein open() function file ka "handle" deta hai — us handle se tum read/write kar sakte ho. Mode batata hai kya karna hai — read karna hai ('r'), write karna hai ('w'), append karna hai ('a').

📋 File Modes Complete Reference:

ModeMeaningFile Exists?File Missing?
'r'Read (default)Opens for readingFileNotFoundError ❌
'w'WriteOVERWRITES ⚠️Creates new
'a'AppendAdds at endCreates new
'x'Exclusive createFileExistsError ❌Creates new
'r+'Read + WriteOpens both opsFileNotFoundError ❌
'w+'Write + ReadOVERWRITES ⚠️Creates new
'rb' / 'wb'Binary modeImages, videosDepends on r/w

💻 Quick Example:

# Basic file operations flow
# Step 1: Open file (get file handle)
file = open("employees.txt", "r")  # mode = read

# Step 2: Read/Write content
content = file.read()
print(content)

# Step 3: ALWAYS close the file!
file.close()

# Check file type
print(type(file))  # <class '_io.TextIOWrapper'>

# ⚠️ If file doesn't exist:
# open("missing.txt", "r") → FileNotFoundError
⚠️ Critical Warnings:
  • 'w' mode DANGER: Existing file ka poora content DELETE kar deta hai! Backup zaroori.
  • File close karna zaroori: Warna resource leak, data loss ho sakta hai.
  • Best practice: Hamesha with open() use karo — auto-close ki guarantee.

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: Text mode aur Binary mode mein kya difference hai?
Ans: Text mode ('r', 'w') — file ko characters/strings ki tarah handle karta hai, encoding (UTF-8 default) apply karta hai, line endings automatically convert karta hai (Windows \\r\\n → \\n). Human-readable files ke liye — .txt, .csv, .json. Binary mode ('rb', 'wb') — raw bytes handle karta hai, no encoding, no line ending conversion. Non-text files ke liye — .jpg, .mp3, .pdf, .exe. Rule: agar file readable text hai → text mode, warna binary mode.

Q: 'w' aur 'a' mode mein kya difference hai?
Ans: 'w' (write): file ka existing content POORA DELETE kar deta hai aur naya content likhta hai. Blank slate. 'a' (append): file ka existing content preserve karta hai, naya content END mein ADD karta hai. Both create file if it doesn't exist. Rule: nayi file ya complete rewrite → 'w', logs/data add karna → 'a'. 'w' data loss ka common cause hai — accidentally important file par 'w' mode use ho jaana.

2. Opening & Closing Files — open(), close() 🟢

📘 Definition: open(filename, mode, encoding) function returns a file object that acts as a handle to the file. Once opened, files MUST be closed using close() to release system resources. Unclosed files can cause memory leaks, data loss, or file lock issues. Best practice: use with statement (covered later) for automatic closing.

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: Basic open() and close()
# Open file for reading
file = open("employees.txt", "r")
print(file.name)      # employees.txt
print(file.mode)      # r
print(file.closed)    # False (open)

# Read something
data = file.read()
print(data)

# Close file — ALWAYS!
file.close()
print(file.closed)    # True (closed now)

# Reading from closed file → ValueError!
# file.read() → ValueError: I/O operation on closed file
# Example 2: open() with encoding parameter
# Default encoding is platform-dependent (usually UTF-8)
file = open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8")
content = file.read()
file.close()

# Reading Hindi/Unicode text — encoding zaroori!
file = open("hindi_data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8")
# Wrong encoding → UnicodeDecodeError

# Common encodings:
# utf-8   → most common, handles all languages
# ascii   → English only, 128 chars
# latin-1 → Western European languages
# cp1252  → Windows default (Western)

# Writing with encoding
file = open("output.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8")
file.write("Namaste Duniya! नमस्ते दुनिया!")
file.close()
# Example 3: Problems with manual close()

# ❌ PROBLEM 1: Forgot to close
file = open("data.txt", "r")
data = file.read()
# close() bhool gaye — resource leak!

# ❌ PROBLEM 2: Exception before close()
file = open("data.txt", "r")
data = file.read()
result = 10 / 0   # ZeroDivisionError!
file.close()      # yeh line kabhi execute nahi hogi ❌

# ✅ SOLUTION 1: try-finally
file = open("data.txt", "r")
try:
    data = file.read()
    # process data...
finally:
    file.close()   # hamesha execute hoga

# ✅ SOLUTION 2 (BEST): with statement — auto-close
with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
    data = file.read()
    # file auto-closes here (even on exception!)
print(file.closed)  # True

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: File close karna kyu zaroori hai?
Ans: Multiple reasons: (1) Resource leak — OS ke pass limited file handles hain, unclosed files handles waste karti hain. (2) Data loss — writes buffer mein rehte hain, close() se disk pe flush hote hain. Without close, data lost ho sakta hai. (3) File lock — Windows mein open file ko dusra program access nahi kar sakta. (4) Memory leak — file object memory occupy karta hai. Solution: with open() statement use karo — automatic close guaranteed, exception ke case mein bhi.

Q: encoding parameter kyu specify karna chahiye?
Ans: Default encoding platform-dependent hai — Windows pe cp1252, Linux pe UTF-8. Yeh cross-platform bugs cause karta hai. Explicit encoding specify karne se: (1) Consistent behavior har OS pe. (2) Unicode characters (Hindi, emoji, special chars) safely handle. (3) UnicodeDecodeError avoid. Best practice: encoding="utf-8" always use karo — modern standard, most languages support karta hai. Legacy files ke liye specific encoding ('latin-1', 'cp1252') use karo.

3. Reading Files — read(), readline(), readlines() 🟢

📘 Definition: Python provides multiple methods to read file content. read(n) reads entire file or n characters. readline() reads one line at a time. readlines() reads all lines into a list. Iterating over file object reads line by line — most memory-efficient for large files.

📋 Reading Methods Comparison:

MethodReturnsMemoryBest For
read()Entire content as stringHigh 🔴Small files
read(n)First n charactersControlledPartial read
readline()Single line (with \\n)Low ⚡Line-by-line processing
readlines()List of all linesHigh 🔴Need all lines as list
for line in fileIterator (lazy)Lowest ⚡⚡BEST — Large files

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: read() — entire file at once
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()
print(content)         # entire file as one string
print(type(content))   # <class 'str'>
print(len(content))    # total characters

# Read only first 50 characters
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    partial = f.read(50)
print(partial)         # first 50 chars only

# ⚠️ Warning: read() loads ENTIRE file in memory
# 10 GB file? 10 GB RAM needed!
# Example 2: readline() and readlines()
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    line1 = f.readline()   # first line (with \\n)
    line2 = f.readline()   # second line
    print(line1.strip())   # strip removes \\n
    print(line2.strip())

# readlines() — ALL lines as list
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
print(type(lines))     # <class 'list'>
print(len(lines))      # number of lines
for line in lines:
    print(line.strip())

# Access specific line
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
print(lines[0])         # first line (header)
print(lines[-1])        # last line
# Example 3: Line-by-line iteration (BEST for large files)
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:               # iterate directly!
        print(line.strip())     # memory-efficient

# Line numbering with enumerate
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    for num, line in enumerate(f, 1):
        print(f"Line {num}: {line.strip()}")
# Line 1: id,name,department,salary
# Line 2: 101,Aarav,IT,55000
# Line 3: 102,Ishita,HR,72000

# Real-world: Search employee in large file
target = "Kabir"
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        if target in line:
            print(f"Found: {line.strip()}")
            break          # stop after first match

# Count lines efficiently
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    line_count = sum(1 for _ in f)
print(f"Total lines: {line_count}")
📋 Which Method When?
• Small file (<10 MB): read() — simple, fast
• Line processing: for line in file — best practice
• Need list of lines: readlines() — only if needed
• Large files (>100 MB): ALWAYS iterate line by line — memory-safe
• 💡 Strip newlines: line.strip() — remove \\n from each line

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: read() vs readlines() vs iterating file — kaunsa better hai?
Ans: Depends on file size aur use case: (1) read() — entire file ek string mein — small files ke liye simple. Memory issue for large files. (2) readlines() — sab lines ki list — memory bhi zyada, no benefit over iteration. (3) for line in file — BEST — lazy iterator, ek waqt mein ek line memory mein, works for GB-sized files. Rule: default choice for line in file — Pythonic, memory-efficient, works everywhere. read() sirf small config files ke liye.

Q: Bade file (10GB) ko efficiently kaise read karo?
Ans: Line-by-line iteration: with open(f) as file: for line in file: — Python lazy iterator use karta hai, sirf current line memory mein. NEVER use read() or readlines() — memory explode ho jaayega. Alternative approaches: (1) Chunk reading: while chunk := f.read(8192): — 8KB chunks. (2) Pandas for CSV: pd.read_csv(chunksize=10000) — process in chunks. (3) Generator functions: yield line by line. (4) mmap module: memory-mapped files for random access. Interview mein "line-by-line iteration" batao — 90% cases mein sufficient.

4. Writing Files — write(), writelines() 🟡

📘 Definition: write(string) writes a single string to file. writelines(list) writes multiple strings from a list — but does NOT add newlines automatically. Mode 'w' overwrites existing content, mode 'a' appends to end. Writes may be buffered — flush() forces immediate write to disk.

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: write() — writing strings
with open("new_employees.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Aarav,IT,55000\n")     # \n zaroori manually!
    f.write("Ishita,HR,72000\n")
    f.write("Kabir,Finance,65000\n")

# write() returns number of characters written
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    count = f.write("Employee added successfully\n")
print(count)  # 28 (characters written)

# Multiple writes
with open("report.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("=== Employee Report ===\n")
    f.write("Date: 2024-01-15\n")
    f.write("Total: 5 employees\n")
    f.write("======================\n")
# Example 2: writelines() — multiple lines from list
employees = [
    "Aarav,IT,55000\n",       # \n manually!
    "Ishita,HR,72000\n",
    "Kabir,Finance,65000\n",
    "Diya,IT,58000\n",
    "Rohan,Marketing,80000\n"
]

with open("employees.txt", "w") as f:
    f.writelines(employees)  # writes all lines

# ⚠️ COMMON TRAP: writelines() doesn't add newlines!
data = ["Aarav", "Ishita", "Kabir"]  # NO \n
with open("bad.txt", "w") as f:
    f.writelines(data)  # result: "AaravIshitaKabir" — all in one line!

# ✅ FIX: add \n to each item
with open("good.txt", "w") as f:
    f.writelines(name + "\n" for name in data)

# ✅ ALTERNATIVE: join with \n
with open("good2.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("\n".join(data))  # cleaner!
# Example 3: Append mode ('a') vs Write mode ('w')

# 'w' mode — OVERWRITES existing content!
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Line 1\n")

with open("log.txt", "w") as f:  # reopen with 'w'
    f.write("Line 2\n")
# File contains only "Line 2" — Line 1 GONE! ⚠️

# 'a' mode — APPENDS to end
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Line 3\n")   # adds at end
    f.write("Line 4\n")
# File now: Line 2, Line 3, Line 4

# Real-world: Logging system
from datetime import datetime
def log_event(message):
    timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
    with open("app.log", "a") as f:
        f.write(f"[{timestamp}] {message}\n")

log_event("Aarav logged in")
log_event("Ishita updated profile")
log_event("Kabir generated report")

# Add employees to existing file
new_emp = ["106,Meera,IT,60000\n", "107,Arjun,HR,68000\n"]
with open("employees.txt", "a") as f:
    f.writelines(new_emp)
⚠️ Common Mistakes:
  • writelines() automatically newline NAHI add karta — manually \\n add karo.
  • 'w' mode existing content DELETE kar deta hai — accidentally important file overwrite mat karo.
  • write() sirf strings accept karta hai — int/float toh str() se convert karo.

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: write() aur writelines() mein kya difference hai?
Ans: write(string) — single string ko file mein likhta hai. writelines(iterable) — iterable (list/tuple) ke saare strings write karta hai. IMPORTANT: writelines() automatically newline NAHI add karta — jaisa data pass karoge waisa hi likha jaayega. Isliye writelines(["a", "b"]) → "ab" (concatenated). Newlines chahiye toh manually add karo — [x + "\\n" for x in list]. Alternative: write("\\n".join(list)) cleaner hai.

Q: 'w' mode ke saath data loss kaise avoid karo?
Ans: Multiple safety approaches: (1) Use 'x' mode — exclusive create, file exist karti hai toh FileExistsError. (2) Check before write: if not os.path.exists(file): open(file, 'w'). (3) Backup first: important files ka backup banao before overwriting. (4) Use 'a' mode — jab possible ho, append safer hai. (5) Write to temp file first: temp file mein likho, phir rename karo. Production code mein always exception handling with try-except use karo write operations ke around.

5. with Statement — Context Manager 🟡

📘 Definition: The with statement is a Context Manager that automatically handles resource cleanup. For files, it guarantees close() is called — even if an exception occurs. Syntax: with open(file) as variable:. This is the RECOMMENDED, Pythonic way to work with files. Avoids resource leaks, ensures clean code, handles exceptions safely.

🎯 Samjho Hinglish Mein: with statement ek "smart guard" hai — jaise ghar mein AC on karke bhool jaao, guard auto-off kar de. File open karo, kaam karo, block khatam hote hi Python automatically close kar deta hai — chahe error aaye ya nahi. Manual close() ki tension nahi. Best practice — HAMESHA with use karo file handling mein. Interview mein manual close likhoge toh negative marks!

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: Traditional vs with statement

# ❌ Traditional way — manual close, error-prone
file = open("employees.txt", "r")
try:
    data = file.read()
    # process data...
finally:
    file.close()

# ✅ Modern way — with statement (BEST PRACTICE)
with open("employees.txt", "r") as file:
    data = file.read()
    # process data...
# file auto-closes here! ✨

# Verify auto-close
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    print(f.closed)   # False (inside with block)
print(f.closed)       # True (outside — auto-closed!)
# Example 2: Exception safety with 'with'

# ❌ Manual close — file leak on exception!
file = open("data.txt", "r")
data = file.read()
result = 10 / 0       # ZeroDivisionError!
file.close()             # yeh line NEVER runs ❌

# ✅ with statement — file closed even on error!
try:
    with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
        data = file.read()
        result = 10 / 0   # exception!
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Error caught, but file was closed properly!")
# file auto-closes even when exception raised
# Example 3: Multiple files with single 'with'

# Read from source, write to destination (file copy)
with open("employees.txt", "r") as src, \
     open("backup.txt", "w") as dst:
    for line in src:
        dst.write(line)
# both files auto-close!

# Python 3.10+ syntax — cleaner
with (
    open("employees.txt", "r") as src,
    open("filtered.txt", "w") as dst
):
    for line in src:
        if "IT" in line:      # filter IT employees only
            dst.write(line)

# Real-world: Process employee report
with open("employees.txt", "r") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()[1:]  # skip header

    total_salary = 0
    for line in lines:
        parts = line.strip().split(",")
        total_salary += int(parts[3])
    
    print(f"Total Salary: ₹{total_salary}")
📋 Why 'with' is Best Practice:
• ✅ Auto-close — file automatically closed
• ✅ Exception safe — closes even on errors
• ✅ Cleaner code — no manual close needed
• ✅ Pythonic — industry standard
• ✅ Works with any resource — files, DB connections, locks
• 💡 Rule: Interview mein file handling likho toh always 'with'!

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: 'with' statement kya hai aur file handling mein kyu use karte hain?
Ans: with statement Python ka Context Manager hai — resources ko safely acquire aur release karta hai. File handling mein: (1) File automatically open hoti hai block start pe, (2) Block khatam hote hi automatically close hoti hai, (3) Exception aaye tab bhi file close hoti hai — __enter__ aur __exit__ methods internally use hote hain. Benefits: manual close() ki zaroorat nahi, resource leaks avoid, cleaner code, exception-safe. Best practice — hamesha use karo file/DB/network operations mein.

Q: 'with' ke bina file close karne mein kya problem hai?
Ans: Problems: (1) Forget close() — coder bhool jaaye toh resource leak. (2) Exception before close() — close() line kabhi execute nahi hogi, file open reh jaayegi. (3) Manual try-finally verbose — code lamba aur ugly. (4) Windows file lock — open file dusra program access nahi kar sakta. Solution — with statement har case handle karta hai automatically. Modern Python code mein manual close almost never use hota. Legacy code ya specific scenarios (long-lived files, multiple functions) mein manual close ho sakta hai.

6. Working with CSV Files — csv Module 🟡

📘 Definition: CSV (Comma-Separated Values) is the most common format for tabular data. Python's built-in csv module provides csv.reader (rows as lists), csv.DictReader (rows as dicts with headers), csv.writer, and csv.DictWriter. Handles quoting, escaping, custom delimiters automatically. For data analysis with millions of rows, prefer Pandas pd.read_csv().

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: Reading CSV with csv.reader
import csv

with open("employees.csv", "r") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)
# ['id', 'name', 'department', 'salary']    ← header
# ['101', 'Aarav', 'IT', '55000']
# ['102', 'Ishita', 'HR', '72000']
# ...

# Access specific columns by index
with open("employees.csv", "r") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    header = next(reader)           # skip header
    for row in reader:
        name = row[1]
        salary = int(row[3])
        print(f"{name}: ₹{salary}")

# Reading with different delimiter (semicolon, tab)
with open("data.tsv", "r") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f, delimiter="\t")
    for row in reader:
        print(row)
# Example 2: DictReader — MORE Pythonic!
import csv

with open("employees.csv", "r") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)
# {'id': '101', 'name': 'Aarav', 'department': 'IT', 'salary': '55000'}
# {'id': '102', 'name': 'Ishita', 'department': 'HR', 'salary': '72000'}
# ...

# Access by column name — no index confusion!
with open("employees.csv", "r") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(f"{row['name']} works in {row['department']}")

# Filter IT department employees
with open("employees.csv", "r") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    it_employees = [row for row in reader if row["department"] == "IT"]
print(f"IT Employees: {len(it_employees)}")

# Calculate total salary by department
from collections import defaultdict
dept_totals = defaultdict(int)
with open("employees.csv", "r") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        dept_totals[row["department"]] += int(row["salary"])
print(dict(dept_totals))
# {'IT': 113000, 'HR': 72000, 'Finance': 65000, 'Marketing': 80000}
# Example 3: Writing CSV files
import csv

# Writing with csv.writer
data = [
    ["id", "name", "department", "salary"],  # header
    [101, "Aarav", "IT", 55000],
    [102, "Ishita", "HR", 72000],
    [103, "Kabir", "Finance", 65000]
]

with open("output.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.writer(f)
    writer.writerows(data)   # write all rows at once
    # writer.writerow(row) — single row

# ⚠️ newline="" IMPORTANT for Windows to avoid extra blank lines!

# Writing with DictWriter (RECOMMENDED)
employees = [
    {"id": 101, "name": "Aarav", "department": "IT", "salary": 55000},
    {"id": 102, "name": "Ishita", "department": "HR", "salary": 72000},
    {"id": 103, "name": "Kabir", "department": "Finance", "salary": 65000}
]

with open("employees_out.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    fieldnames = ["id", "name", "department", "salary"]
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fieldnames)
    writer.writeheader()          # writes column names
    writer.writerows(employees)   # writes all data

# Append new employee to existing CSV
new_emp = {"id": 104, "name": "Diya", "department": "IT", "salary": 58000}
with open("employees_out.csv", "a", newline="") as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fieldnames)
    writer.writerow(new_emp)      # single row append
⚠️ CSV Writing Tips:
  • newline="" parameter ZAROORI hai writing time — Windows pe extra blank lines avoid karne ke liye.
  • All values automatically string mein convert hote hain — reading time pe int/float manually convert karo.
  • Special characters (comma, quote) automatically escape hote hain by csv module.

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: csv.reader vs csv.DictReader — kaunsa better hai?
Ans: csv.reader rows ko lists ke roop mein deta hai — index se access row[0]. Simple, fast. csv.DictReader rows ko dicts mein deta hai using headers as keys — row["name"]. Advantages: (1) Column order change ho toh code nahi tootega. (2) Self-documenting — column name se access clear hai. (3) Missing/extra columns handle karne mein flexible. Disadvantages: Thoda slow (dict creation overhead), memory zyada. Rule: real-world code mein DictReader preferred — readability jyada important hai. Performance critical case mein csv.reader.

Q: Bade CSV files (1GB+) ke liye kya use karo — csv module ya Pandas?
Ans: Depends on use case: (1) Simple line-by-line processing — csv module use karo, memory efficient (iterator based). (2) Data analysis, filtering, aggregation — Pandas pd.read_csv() with chunksize parameter. (3) Massive files (10GB+) — Dask, PyArrow, or Vaex — parallel processing, lazy loading. Rule: analytics chahiye toh Pandas, streaming/basic ops chahiye toh csv module. chunksize parameter Pandas mein magic hai — memory manageable rakhta hai.

7. Working with JSON Files — json Module 🟡

📘 Definition: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard data exchange format — used in APIs, config files, NoSQL databases. Python's json module provides 4 main functions — json.load() (file → dict), json.loads() (string → dict), json.dump() (dict → file), json.dumps() (dict → string). JSON maps naturally to Python dict/list/str/int/float/bool/None.

📋 JSON ↔ Python Type Mapping:

JSONPython
object {}dict
array []list
stringstr
number (int)int
number (real)float
true / falseTrue / False
nullNone

💻 Examples:

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: json.dump() vs json.dumps() — kya difference hai?
Ans: Naming convention — 's' means string. (1) json.dump(obj, file) — Python object ko JSON format mein FILE mein likhta hai. (2) json.dumps(obj) — Python object ko JSON STRING mein convert karta hai (returns string). Similarly json.load(file) file se, json.loads(string) string se. Use case: dump/load file operations ke liye, dumps/loads string manipulation (API responses, network data) ke liye. Memory: dump direct file mein, dumps memory mein string banata hai.

Q: JSON mein Python ki tuple, set, datetime kaise handle karo?
Ans: JSON natively support NAHI karta yeh types: (1) Tuple → auto-convert to list — (1,2) becomes [1,2], roundtrip mein list rahega. (2) Set → TypeError, manually list mein convert karo. (3) Datetime → TypeError, isoformat string mein convert karo: dt.isoformat(). (4) Custom classes → TypeError, custom encoder chahiye. Solutions: (1) json.dumps(data, default=str) — unknown types ko string mein force convert. (2) Custom encoder class banao inheriting json.JSONEncoder. (3) Data preparation step add karo before serialization.

8. File Paths — os & pathlib 🔴

📘 Definition: File paths differ between operating systems — Windows uses \, Linux/Mac use /. os.path module (older) provides path manipulation functions. pathlib module (Python 3.4+, MODERN) provides object-oriented Path class with cleaner API. Both handle cross-platform paths correctly. Modern code should prefer pathlib.

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: os.path — traditional approach
import os

# Current working directory
cwd = os.getcwd()
print(cwd)  # C:\Users\Aarav\Projects (Windows) or /home/aarav/projects (Linux)

# Cross-platform path building
path = os.path.join("data", "employees", "file.csv")
print(path)  # data\employees\file.csv OR data/employees/file.csv

# Check file existence
if os.path.exists("employees.csv"):
    print("File exists!")
else:
    print("File not found")

# File properties
if os.path.exists("employees.csv"):
    print(os.path.isfile("employees.csv"))     # True
    print(os.path.isdir("employees.csv"))      # False
    print(os.path.getsize("employees.csv"))     # file size in bytes
    print(os.path.abspath("employees.csv"))     # absolute path
    print(os.path.dirname("data/employees.csv"))  # 'data'
    print(os.path.basename("data/employees.csv")) # 'employees.csv'
    print(os.path.splitext("employees.csv"))     # ('employees', '.csv')

# List directory contents
files = os.listdir(".")  # current directory
print(files)
# Example 2: pathlib — MODERN & RECOMMENDED
from pathlib import Path

# Create Path object
p = Path("employees.csv")
print(p)             # employees.csv
print(p.name)        # employees.csv
print(p.stem)        # employees (filename without extension)
print(p.suffix)      # .csv
print(p.parent)      # . (parent directory)

# Check existence & type
print(p.exists())    # True/False
print(p.is_file())   # True if regular file
print(p.is_dir())    # True if directory

# Build paths using / operator (SUPER CLEAN!)
data_dir = Path("data")
file_path = data_dir / "employees" / "file.csv"
print(file_path)     # data\employees\file.csv (auto cross-platform!)

# Absolute path
print(p.absolute())  # full path from root

# Read/write directly (Path has these methods!)
Path("note.txt").write_text("Aarav joined IT")
content = Path("note.txt").read_text()
print(content)  # Aarav joined IT

# List directory contents
for item in Path(".").iterdir():
    print(item)

# Find files matching pattern (glob)
csv_files = list(Path(".").glob("*.csv"))
print(csv_files)  # all .csv files in current dir

# Recursive search (all subdirs)
all_py = list(Path(".").rglob("*.py"))
print(all_py)
# Example 3: Directory operations & real-world
from pathlib import Path
import os

# Create directory
Path("reports").mkdir(exist_ok=True)   # don't fail if exists
Path("data/2024/january").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
# parents=True creates all missing parent dirs

# Remove file
Path("old.txt").unlink(missing_ok=True)  # won't error if missing

# Remove empty directory
Path("reports").rmdir()   # only works if empty

# Rename/move file
Path("old.csv").rename("new.csv")

# Real-world: Organize employee reports by department
from pathlib import Path
import csv

# Read employees
with open("employees.csv", "r") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    employees = list(reader)

# Create folder for each department, save employees inside
for emp in employees:
    dept_folder = Path("departments") / emp["department"]
    dept_folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    
    emp_file = dept_folder / f"{emp['name']}.txt"
    emp_file.write_text(f"ID: {emp['id']}\nSalary: {emp['salary']}")

# Result:
# departments/IT/Aarav.txt
# departments/HR/Ishita.txt
# departments/Finance/Kabir.txt
# departments/IT/Diya.txt
# departments/Marketing/Rohan.txt

# Get script's own directory
script_dir = Path(__file__).parent  # where this .py file lives
data_path = script_dir / "data" / "employees.csv"
# works from any location — absolute path resolved
📋 os.path vs pathlib:
• os.path — string-based, older API, functions like os.path.join()
• pathlib — object-oriented, modern (3.4+), uses / operator
• Same functionality, different style — pathlib more Pythonic
• Interoperable — str(path_obj) converts to string for old APIs
• 💡 Modern code mein hamesha pathlib use karo — cleaner, safer, more features

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: pathlib aur os.path mein kaunsa use karo aur kyu?
Ans: pathlib PREFERRED hai (Python 3.4+) — modern, cleaner. Benefits: (1) Object-oriented — Path objects have methods like .exists(), .read_text(). (2) / operator for joining — Path("a") / "b" / "c" — more readable than os.path.join("a","b","c"). (3) Cross-platform automatic. (4) Better semantic methods — .stem, .suffix, .parent. (5) Direct file I/O — .write_text(), .read_text(). Use os.path only for legacy code compatibility ya specific edge cases. Modern Python code should use pathlib.

Q: Cross-platform paths kaise handle karte hain?
Ans: Windows aur Linux mein path separator different hain (\ vs /). Solutions: (1) NEVER hardcode separators — "data\\file.csv" Windows-specific. (2) Use os.path.join() or pathlib / — automatically correct separator. (3) Use raw strings for Windows literals — r"C:\Users". (4) Forward slash works everywhere — Python 3 mein Windows bhi / accept karta hai in most cases. Best practice: pathlib ka / operator use karo — Path("data") / "employees" / "file.csv" — works on all OS, cleaner code.

9. Exception Handling — try, except, else, finally 🔴

📘 Definition: Exception Handling is the mechanism to handle runtime errors gracefully without crashing the program. Syntax: try (risky code) → except (handle error) → else (runs if no error) → finally (always runs — cleanup). Prevents program termination, allows recovery, logs errors, ensures resource cleanup. Essential for production code.

🎯 Samjho Hinglish Mein: Exception = runtime error — program chalate waqt jab kuch galat ho jaaye (file missing, wrong input, division by zero). Without handling — program CRASH ho jaayega. try-except = safety net — risky code try karo, error aaye toh gracefully handle karo, program continue rahega. Real-world: user input, file operations, API calls — sab risky hain, exception handling zaroori hai. Interview mein must-know topic.

📋 try-except-else-finally Flow:

try:
    # Risky code — may raise exception
    result = risky_operation()
except SomeError:
    # Runs IF exception occurs
    handle_error()
else:
    # Runs IF NO exception (optional)
    print("Success!")
finally:
    # ALWAYS runs — cleanup code (optional)
    cleanup()

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: Basic try-except

# ❌ Without exception handling — CRASH!
# result = 10 / 0  → ZeroDivisionError, program terminates

# ✅ With exception handling — graceful
try:
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Cannot divide by zero!")
    result = 0
print(f"Result: {result}")  # Program continues!

# File not found handling
try:
    with open("missing.csv", "r") as f:
        data = f.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found — using default")
    data = ""

# Get exception details
try:
    num = int("Aarav")
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")          # Error: invalid literal for int()
    print(f"Type: {type(e).__name__}")  # Type: ValueError
# Example 2: Multiple except blocks

def process_salary(filename, employee_name):
    try:
        with open(filename, "r") as f:
            data = f.read()
        salary_str = data.split(",")[3]
        salary = int(salary_str)
        return salary
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"❌ File '{filename}' not found")
    except IndexError:
        print("❌ Invalid file format")
    except ValueError:
        print("❌ Salary is not a valid number")
    except Exception as e:      # catch-all for unknown
        print(f"❌ Unexpected error: {e}")
    return None

# Multiple exceptions in single except
try:
    value = int(input("Enter salary: "))
    result = 100 / value
except (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError) as e:
    print(f"Invalid input: {e}")
# Example 3: else and finally clauses

def read_employee_file(filename):
    file = None
    try:
        file = open(filename, "r")
        data = file.read()
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print("File not found")
        return None
    else:
        # Runs ONLY if try succeeded (no exception)
        print(f"✅ Successfully read {len(data)} chars")
        return data
    finally:
        # ALWAYS runs — cleanup!
        if file is not None:
            file.close()
            print("🔒 File closed")

# Real-world: Robust CSV processor with all clauses
import csv

def process_employees(filename):
    valid_rows = []
    error_count = 0
    
    try:
        with open(filename, "r") as f:
            reader = csv.DictReader(f)
            for row_num, row in enumerate(reader, 2):
                try:
                    row["salary"] = int(row["salary"])
                    valid_rows.append(row)
                except (ValueError, KeyError) as e:
                    print(f"Row {row_num}: {e}")
                    error_count += 1
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"File '{filename}' does not exist")
        return [], 0
    except PermissionError:
        print("No permission to read file")
        return [], 0
    else:
        print(f"✅ Processing complete")
    finally:
        print(f"📊 Valid: {len(valid_rows)}, Errors: {error_count}")
    
    return valid_rows, error_count

employees, errors = process_employees("employees.csv")
⚠️ Common Mistakes:
  • Bare except — except: without exception name catches EVERYTHING including SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt. Always specify exception type.
  • Overly broad except — except Exception: catches too much, hides real bugs. Be specific.
  • Silent failures — except: pass — errors ignore ho jaate hain, debugging nightmare!

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: try-except-else-finally ka execution order kya hai?
Ans: Order: (1) try block execute hota hai. (2) If exception occurs → matching except block runs, else skips. (3) If NO exception → else block runs (skipped on exception). (4) finally ALWAYS runs — success ho ya exception. Real behavior: try succeeds → try → else → finally. Try fails → try → except → finally. finally hamesha last mein, chahe exception handle ho ya na ho. Use case: else — success-only actions, finally — cleanup (file close, DB disconnect).

Q: except aur except Exception mein kya farak hai?
Ans: Bare except: — catches ALL exceptions including system-level ones (SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt) — DANGEROUS! User Ctrl+C nahi kar sakta, script kill nahi hoti. except Exception: — catches all user-level exceptions but ALLOWS system exits — safer. Best practice: hamesha specific exception catch karo — except FileNotFoundError:, except ValueError:. Multiple specific except blocks better hain than one broad. Broad exception sirf last resort mein use karo — with logging aur re-raise.

10. Common Built-in Exceptions 🔴

📘 Definition: Python provides 60+ built-in exception classes for common error scenarios. All inherit from BaseException. Most user code deals with subclasses of Exception. Understanding common exceptions helps write robust error handling. Each exception represents a specific error type — file missing (FileNotFoundError), invalid conversion (ValueError), wrong type operation (TypeError), etc.

📋 Most Common Exceptions:

ExceptionWhen OccursExample
FileNotFoundErrorFile doesn't existopen("missing.txt")
ValueErrorRight type, wrong valueint("abc")
TypeErrorWrong type used"5" + 5
KeyErrorDict key missingd["missing"]
IndexErrorList index out of rangelst[100]
ZeroDivisionErrorDivision by zero10 / 0
AttributeErrorObject lacks attribute"hi".invalid()
PermissionErrorAccess deniedRead-only file write
ImportErrorModule not foundimport fakemodule
NameErrorVariable not definedprint(undefined)

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: File-related exceptions
try:
    with open("missing.csv", "r") as f:
        data = f.read()
except FileNotFoundError as e:
    print(f"FileNotFoundError: {e}")
except PermissionError as e:
    print(f"PermissionError: {e}")
except IsADirectoryError:
    print("Path is directory, not file")

# Type conversion exceptions
try:
    salary = int("fifty thousand")  # ValueError
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Cannot convert: {e}")

try:
    result = "Aarav" + 100       # TypeError
except TypeError as e:
    print(f"Type mismatch: {e}")

# Collection exceptions
employees = {"Aarav": 55000, "Ishita": 72000}
try:
    salary = employees["Rohan"]      # KeyError
except KeyError as e:
    print(f"Key not found: {e}")

names = ["Aarav", "Ishita", "Kabir"]
try:
    print(names[10])           # IndexError
except IndexError as e:
    print(f"Index out of range: {e}")
# Example 2: Exception hierarchy
# BaseException
#   ├── SystemExit
#   ├── KeyboardInterrupt
#   └── Exception
#         ├── ArithmeticError
#         │     ├── ZeroDivisionError
#         │     └── OverflowError
#         ├── LookupError
#         │     ├── KeyError
#         │     └── IndexError
#         ├── OSError
#         │     ├── FileNotFoundError
#         │     └── PermissionError
#         ├── ValueError
#         └── TypeError

# Catching parent catches all children
try:
    d = {"a": 1}
    print(d["b"])       # KeyError
except LookupError:      # catches KeyError AND IndexError
    print("Lookup failed")

try:
    result = 10 / 0
except ArithmeticError:   # catches all math errors
    print("Math error occurred")

try:
    open("missing.txt")
except OSError:          # catches file/OS errors
    print("OS operation failed")
# Example 3: Real-world employee data validator
def validate_employee_data(row):
    errors = []
    
    try:
        emp_id = int(row["id"])
        if emp_id <= 0:
            errors.append("ID must be positive")
    except KeyError:
        errors.append("Missing 'id' field")
    except ValueError:
        errors.append("ID must be a number")
    
    try:
        salary = int(row["salary"])
        if salary < 0:
            errors.append("Salary cannot be negative")
    except KeyError:
        errors.append("Missing 'salary' field")
    except ValueError:
        errors.append("Salary must be a number")
    
    try:
        name = row["name"].strip()
        if not name:
            errors.append("Name cannot be empty")
    except KeyError:
        errors.append("Missing 'name' field")
    except AttributeError:
        errors.append("Name must be string")
    
    return errors

# Test data
test_rows = [
    {"id": "101", "name": "Aarav", "salary": "55000"},   # valid
    {"id": "abc", "name": "Ishita", "salary": "72000"},  # bad id
    {"id": "102", "salary": "-1000"},                # missing name, negative salary
]

for i, row in enumerate(test_rows, 1):
    errors = validate_employee_data(row)
    if errors:
        print(f"Row {i} errors: {errors}")
    else:
        print(f"Row {i}: ✅ Valid")

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: ValueError aur TypeError mein kya difference hai?
Ans: ValueError — sahi TYPE but galat VALUE. Type toh acceptable hai, but us specific value ke saath operation possible nahi. Example: int("abc") — string type valid hai int() ke liye, but "abc" convert nahi ho sakta. TypeError — TYPE hi galat use ho raha hai. Operation supported nahi hai us type ke liye. Example: "5" + 5 — string aur int add nahi ho sakte. Rule of thumb: type acceptable + wrong value → ValueError, type itself wrong → TypeError.

Q: Exception hierarchy kaise use karte hain?
Ans: Python exceptions ek tree structure follow karti hain — BaseException → Exception → specific errors. Parent catch karo, sab children catch honge. Example: except LookupError catches both KeyError aur IndexError. except OSError catches FileNotFoundError, PermissionError, etc. Use cases: (1) Broad category handling — ArithmeticError for all math errors. (2) Specific handling — ValueError vs TypeError. (3) Catch-all fallback — except Exception at end. Best practice: specific first, broad last. Order matters — Python first matching except execute karta hai.

11. Raising Exceptions — raise Keyword 🔴

📘 Definition: The raise statement manually triggers an exception. Use it to enforce constraints, validate input, signal errors, or re-raise caught exceptions. Syntax: raise ExceptionType("message"). Can also re-raise: raise alone re-raises current exception. Chained exceptions: raise NewError from original_error preserves context.

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: Basic raise for validation
def set_salary(salary):
    if not isinstance(salary, (int, float)):
        raise TypeError("Salary must be a number")
    if salary < 0:
        raise ValueError("Salary cannot be negative")
    if salary > 10000000:
        raise ValueError("Salary exceeds maximum limit")
    return salary

# Test
try:
    set_salary(-1000)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")   # Error: Salary cannot be negative

# Age validation
def register_employee(name, age):
    if not name or not name.strip():
        raise ValueError("Name cannot be empty")
    if age < 18:
        raise ValueError(f"Age must be 18+, got {age}")
    if age > 70:
        raise ValueError(f"Age must be under 70, got {age}")
    return f"Registered {name} ({age})"

try:
    register_employee("", 25)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Registration failed: {e}")
# Example 2: Re-raising exceptions
def process_file(filename):
    try:
        with open(filename, "r") as f:
            data = f.read()
        return data
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"⚠️ Logging: File missing — {filename}")
        raise   # re-raise same exception to caller

# Caller sees original error
try:
    data = process_file("missing.csv")
except FileNotFoundError as e:
    print(f"Handled in main: {e}")

# Chained exceptions — 'raise from'
def get_employee_salary(emp_id):
    employees = {101: 55000, 102: 72000}
    try:
        return employees[emp_id]
    except KeyError as e:
        # Chain with original exception
        raise ValueError(f"Employee {emp_id} not in database") from e

try:
    get_employee_salary(999)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    print(f"Caused by: {e.__cause__}")
# Error: Employee 999 not in database
# Caused by: 999
# Example 3: Real-world validation pipeline
import csv

def validate_row(row, row_num):
    # Required fields check
    required = ["id", "name", "department", "salary"]
    for field in required:
        if field not in row or not row[field].strip():
            raise ValueError(f"Row {row_num}: Missing '{field}'")
    
    # Type validation
    try:
        row["id"] = int(row["id"])
        row["salary"] = int(row["salary"])
    except ValueError as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Row {row_num}: Invalid number - {e}") from e
    
    # Business rules
    if row["salary"] < 10000:
        raise ValueError(f"Row {row_num}: Salary too low")
    
    valid_depts = ["IT", "HR", "Finance", "Marketing"]
    if row["department"] not in valid_depts:
        raise ValueError(f"Row {row_num}: Invalid dept '{row['department']}'")
    
    return row

def process_csv(filename):
    valid = []
    errors = []
    with open(filename, "r") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        for row_num, row in enumerate(reader, 2):
            try:
                validated = validate_row(row, row_num)
                valid.append(validated)
            except ValueError as e:
                errors.append(str(e))
    return valid, errors

# Usage
valid, errors = process_csv("employees.csv")
print(f"✅ Valid: {len(valid)} employees")
print(f"❌ Errors: {len(errors)}")
for err in errors:
    print(f"  {err}")

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: raise ka use kya hai aur kab karte hain?
Ans: raise statement manually exception trigger karta hai. Use cases: (1) Input validation — invalid parameters pe error raise karo. (2) Business rules — negative salary, invalid age pe rules enforce karo. (3) State validation — object state invalid ho toh error. (4) Re-raising — caught exception ko wapas raise karo caller ke liye. (5) Custom exceptions — domain-specific errors trigger karo. Syntax: raise ExceptionType("message"). Best practice: descriptive message do, context include karo (values, IDs), appropriate exception type choose karo (ValueError, TypeError).

Q: raise aur raise from mein kya difference hai?
Ans: raise — same exception ko wapas throw karta hai (re-raise). Original traceback preserve rehta hai. raise NewException from OldException — exception CHAINING — new exception raise karta hai but old exception ko cause ke roop mein link karta hai. Benefits: (1) Full context preserve. (2) Debugging easy — original error kya tha aur wrapper mein kaise convert hua. (3) Traceback mein "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception" show hota hai. Use case: low-level errors ko high-level meaningful errors mein wrap karna, without losing original context. Access via exception.__cause__.

12. Custom Exceptions — User-Defined Errors 🔴

📘 Definition: Custom Exceptions are user-defined exception classes for domain-specific errors. Create by inheriting from Exception (or its subclasses). Provides clearer error semantics, better categorization, and specific error handling. Best practice: inherit from most specific relevant exception, add custom attributes/methods, use descriptive names ending with "Error".

🎯 Samjho Hinglish Mein: Built-in exceptions general hain — ValueError, TypeError. But real-world mein domain-specific errors chahiye — InvalidSalaryError, EmployeeNotFoundError. Custom exceptions banake tum apne code ki language mein errors describe karte ho. Cleaner code, better error handling, self-documenting. Bade projects mein sabhi frameworks (Django, Flask, FastAPI) custom exceptions use karte hain.

💻 Examples:

# Example 1: Basic custom exception
class EmployeeNotFoundError(Exception):
    """Raised when employee doesn't exist in database"""
    pass

class InvalidSalaryError(Exception):
    """Raised when salary value is invalid"""
    pass

# Use custom exceptions
def get_employee(emp_id):
    employees = {101: "Aarav", 102: "Ishita", 103: "Kabir"}
    if emp_id not in employees:
        raise EmployeeNotFoundError(f"Employee {emp_id} not found")
    return employees[emp_id]

def update_salary(emp_id, new_salary):
    if new_salary < 0:
        raise InvalidSalaryError(f"Salary cannot be negative: {new_salary}")
    return f"Updated {emp_id} to ₹{new_salary}"

# Handle specific errors
try:
    emp = get_employee(999)
except EmployeeNotFoundError as e:
    print(f"❌ {e}")

try:
    update_salary(101, -1000)
except InvalidSalaryError as e:
    print(f"❌ {e}")
# Example 2: Custom exception with attributes
class SalaryLimitError(Exception):
    """Raised when salary exceeds/below limits"""
    def __init__(self, salary, min_limit, max_limit):
        self.salary = salary
        self.min_limit = min_limit
        self.max_limit = max_limit
        message = (
            f"Salary ₹{salary} out of range "
            f"[₹{min_limit} - ₹{max_limit}]"
        )
        super().__init__(message)

def set_salary_with_limits(salary):
    MIN, MAX = 15000, 500000
    if salary < MIN or salary > MAX:
        raise SalaryLimitError(salary, MIN, MAX)
    return salary

try:
    set_salary_with_limits(5000)
except SalaryLimitError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    print(f"Attempted: ₹{e.salary}")
    print(f"Range: ₹{e.min_limit}-₹{e.max_limit}")
# Error: Salary ₹5000 out of range [₹15000 - ₹500000]
# Attempted: ₹5000
# Range: ₹15000-₹500000
# Example 3: Exception hierarchy for large app

# Base exception for module
class EmployeeError(Exception):
    """Base class for all employee-related errors"""
    pass

# Specific exception subclasses
class EmployeeNotFoundError(EmployeeError):
    """Employee doesn't exist"""
    pass

class DuplicateEmployeeError(EmployeeError):
    """Employee ID already exists"""
    pass

class InvalidDepartmentError(EmployeeError):
    """Invalid department name"""
    pass

class SalaryError(EmployeeError):
    """Base for salary-related errors"""
    pass

class NegativeSalaryError(SalaryError):
    pass

class ExcessiveSalaryError(SalaryError):
    pass

# Employee management class
class EmployeeManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.employees = {}
        self.valid_depts = {"IT", "HR", "Finance", "Marketing"}
    
    def add_employee(self, emp_id, name, dept, salary):
        if emp_id in self.employees:
            raise DuplicateEmployeeError(f"Employee {emp_id} exists")
        if dept not in self.valid_depts:
            raise InvalidDepartmentError(f"Unknown dept: {dept}")
        if salary < 0:
            raise NegativeSalaryError(f"Negative salary: {salary}")
        if salary > 1000000:
            raise ExcessiveSalaryError(f"Excessive salary: {salary}")
        self.employees[emp_id] = {"name": name, "dept": dept, "salary": salary}
    
    def get_employee(self, emp_id):
        if emp_id not in self.employees:
            raise EmployeeNotFoundError(f"No employee {emp_id}")
        return self.employees[emp_id]

# Usage with hierarchy-based catching
mgr = EmployeeManager()
try:
    mgr.add_employee(101, "Aarav", "XYZ", 55000)
except SalaryError as e:       # catches ALL salary errors
    print(f"Salary issue: {e}")
except EmployeeError as e:     # catches ALL employee errors
    print(f"Employee issue: {e}")
📋 Custom Exception Best Practices:
• Name ends with "Error" — InvalidSalaryError, not InvalidSalary
• Inherit from Exception or specific subclass — NEVER from BaseException
• Add docstring — explain when this exception is raised
• Create hierarchy — base class + specific subclasses for large apps
• Custom attributes — self.value, self.field for context
• 💡 Custom exceptions = better code documentation aur error handling

💬 Interview Q&A:

Q: Custom exceptions kab aur kyu banate hain?
Ans: Custom exceptions banate hain when: (1) Domain-specific errors — EmployeeNotFoundError more meaningful than generic KeyError. (2) Better categorization — grouping related errors under common parent (SalaryError → NegativeSalaryError, ExcessiveSalaryError). (3) Specific handling — catch specific error types differently in code. (4) Framework/library development — provide clear error API to users. (5) Documentation — self-documenting code. Benefits: cleaner error messages, better debugging, structured error handling, professional code quality. Sab modern frameworks (Django, FastAPI, requests) heavy custom exceptions use karte hain.

Q: Exception hierarchy design mein kya considerations hain?
Ans: Design principles: (1) Base class per module/domain — EmployeeError as root. (2) Category subclasses — SalaryError, DepartmentError. (3) Specific leaf classes — NegativeSalaryError. (4) Inherit from most relevant built-in — if it's a value issue → inherit from ValueError. (5) Consistent naming — all end with "Error". Benefits: (1) User can catch specific → except NegativeSalaryError. (2) User can catch category → except SalaryError catches all salary issues. (3) User can catch everything → except EmployeeError. Follows Python's own exception hierarchy pattern (OSError → FileNotFoundError, PermissionError).

13. Best Practices & Summary 📋

📘 Definition: Following best practices for file handling and exception management leads to robust, maintainable, and production-ready code. This section summarizes key patterns, common mistakes to avoid, and provides a comprehensive cheat sheet for daily reference.

📋 File Handling Best Practices:

✅ DO❌ DON'T
Use with open() for auto-closeManual file.close()
Specify encoding — encoding="utf-8"Rely on default encoding
Iterate large files line-by-lineread() huge files fully
Use pathlib.Path for pathsHardcode / or \
